chapters.title: Chapter 1 - Introduction
chapters.content:
The Time Traveller (for so it will be convenient to speak of him) was expounding a recondite matter to us. His grey eyes shone and twinkled, and his usually pale face was flushed and animated. The fire burnt brightly, and the soft radiance of the incandescent lights in the lilies of silver caught the bubbles that flashed and passed in our glasses. Our chairs, being his patents, embraced and caressed us rather than submitted to be sat upon, and there was that luxurious after-dinner atmosphere, when thought runs gracefully free of the trammels of precision. And he put it to us in this way—marking the points with a lean forefinger—as we sat and lazily admired his earnestness over this new paradox (as we thought it) and his fecundity.

“You must follow me carefully. I shall have to controvert one or two ideas that are almost universally accepted. The geometry, for instance, they taught you at school is founded on a misconception.”

“Is not that rather a large thing to expect us to begin upon?” said Filby, an argumentative person with red hair.

“I do not mean to ask you to accept anything without reasonable ground for it. You will soon admit as much as I need from you. You know of course that a mathematical line, a line of thickness nil, has no real existence. They taught you that? Neither has a mathematical plane. These things are mere abstractions.”

“That is all right,” said the Psychologist.

“Nor, having only length, breadth, and thickness, can a cube have a real existence.”

“There I object,” said Filby. “Of course a solid body may exist. All real things—”

“So most people think. But wait a moment. Can an instantaneous cube exist?”

“Don’t follow you,” said Filby.

“Can a cube that does not last for any time at all, have a real existence?”

Filby became pensive. “Clearly,” the Time Traveller proceeded, “any real body must have extension in four directions: it must have Length, Breadth, Thickness, and—Duration. But through a natural infirmity of the flesh, which I will explain to you in a moment, we incline to overlook this fact.

chapters.title: Chapter 2 - The Machine
chapters.content:
The thing the Time Traveller held in his hand was a glittering metallic framework, scarcely larger than a small clock, and very delicately made. There was ivory in it, and some transparent crystalline substance. And now I must be explicit, for this that follows—unless his explanation is to be accepted—is an absolutely unaccountable thing. He took one of the small octagonal tables that were scattered about the room, and set it in front of the fire, with two legs on the hearthrug. On this table he placed the mechanism. Then he drew up a chair, and sat down. The only other object on the table was a small shaded lamp, the bright light of which fell full upon the model. There were also perhaps a dozen candles about, two in brass candlesticks upon the mantel and several in sconces, so that the room was brilliantly illuminated. I sat in a low arm-chair nearest the fire, and I drew this forward so as to be almost between the Time Traveller and the fireplace. Filby sat behind him, looking over his shoulder. The Medical Man and the Provincial Mayor watched him in profile from the right, the Psychologist from the left. The Very Young Man stood behind the Psychologist. We were all on the alert. It appears incredible to me that any kind of trick, however subtly conceived and however adroitly done, could have been played upon us under these conditions.

The Time Traveller looked at us, and then at the mechanism. “Well?” said the Psychologist.

“This little affair,” said the Time Traveller, resting his elbows upon the table and pressing his hands together above the apparatus, “is only a model. It is my plan for a machine to travel through time. You will notice that it looks singularly askew, and that there is an odd twinkling appearance about this bar, as though it was in some way unreal.” He pointed to the part with his finger. “Also, here is one little white lever, and here is another.”

The Medical Man got up out of his chair and peered into the thing. “It’s beautifully made,” he said.

“It took two years to make,” retorted the Time Traveller.

chapters.title: Chapter 1 - Introduction
chapters.content:
Husain The Time Traveller (as I will call him for convenience) was explaining a difficult subject to us. His grey eyes sparkled, and his usually pale face was flushed with excitement. The fire burned brightly, and the soft glow of the electric lights in the silver lily-shaped lamps caught the bubbles that shimmered and disappeared in our glasses. Our chairs, which he had designed himself, seemed to embrace and support us rather than simply hold us. The room had that comfortable, luxurious feeling that comes after dinner, when the mind can wander freely without having to be precise. This was how he explained his idea to us, emphasizing each point with his slender forefinger. We sat back, casually admiring his enthusiasm for this new paradox (as we thought of it) and his remarkable imagination.

“You must follow me carefully. I will have to challenge one or two ideas that almost everyone accepts as true. Take geometry, for example. The geometry you learned at school is based on a misunderstanding.”

“Isn’t that rather a big idea to expect us to accept right from the start?” said Filby, a red-haired man who loved to argue.

“I am not asking you to accept anything without good reason. You will soon agree with everything I need you to understand. You know, of course, that a mathematical line—a line with no thickness at all—does not really exist. They taught you that, didn’t they? The same is true of a mathematical plane. These things are simply abstract ideas.”

“That’s all right,” said the Psychologist.

“And since a cube has only length, width, and height, it cannot truly exist either.”

“I disagree,” said Filby. “Of course a solid object can exist. All real things—”

“That’s what most people think. But wait a moment. Can a cube that exists for only an instant really exist?”

“I don’t follow you,” said Filby.

“Can a cube that lasts for no time at all have any real existence?”

Filby fell silent, thinking. “Clearly,” the Time Traveller continued, “every real object must extend in four dimensions. It must have Length, Width, Height, and—Duration. But because of a natural limitation of the human body, which I will explain in a moment, we tend to overlook this fact.

chapters.title: Chapter 2 - The Machine
chapters.content:
The Time Traveller held a small, carefully made device in his hand. It had a shiny metal frame and was no larger than a small clock. It contained ivory and some kind of transparent, crystal-like material. Now I must explain what happened next clearly, because unless we accept his explanation, it seems impossible to account for.

He picked up one of the small octagonal tables scattered around the room and placed it in front of the fire, with two of its legs resting on the hearthrug. He set the mechanism on the table, pulled up a chair, and sat down. The only other thing on the table was a small shaded lamp. Its bright light shone directly onto the model. There were perhaps a dozen candles around the room as well. Two stood in brass candlesticks on the mantelpiece, and several others were fixed in wall sconces. Together, they lit the room brilliantly.

I was sitting in a low armchair nearest the fire. I pulled it forward until I was almost between the Time Traveller and the fireplace. Filby sat behind him, looking over his shoulder. The Medical Man and the Provincial Mayor watched him from the side on his right, while the Psychologist watched from his left. The Very Young Man stood behind the Psychologist. We were all alert and watching closely. It still seems impossible to me that anyone could have fooled us under those circumstances, no matter how cleverly the trick had been planned or how skillfully it had been performed.

The Time Traveller looked at us, then at the mechanism.

“Well?” said the Psychologist.

“This little device,” said the Time Traveller, resting his elbows on the table and bringing his hands together above the apparatus, “is only a model. It shows my design for a machine that can travel through time. You’ll notice that it looks unusually crooked, and that this bar has a strange, flickering appearance, as if it weren’t quite real.”

He pointed to that part with his finger.

“There is also a small white lever here, and another one over here.”

The Medical Man stood up and leaned closer to examine it.

“It’s beautifully made,” he said.

“It took two years to make,” replied the Time Traveller.
